reason: The wording and the locator are right and the refutation is not about either. I pulled the whole of ST 7 from davidhume.org and the sentence is verbatim, colon and capital It and semicolon intact, at ST 7, Mil 229 to 30. What breaks is the context, and the verifier's own evidence shows how it broke: it describes ST 7 as “the paragraph arguing that a thousand different sentiments excited by the same object are all right”, as though Hume were arguing it. He is not. ST 7 opens “There is a species of philosophy, which cuts off all hopes of success in such an attempt, and represents the impossibility of ever attaining any standard of taste”, and its second sentence carries the tell: “The difference, IT IS SAID, is very wide between judgment and sentiment.” Everything after that, the thousand sentiments, the Beauty sentence, the real sweet and real bitter, is Hume voicing that species of philosophy. ST 8 then turns on it: “But though this axiom, by passing into a proverb, seems to have attained the sanction of common sense; there is certainly a species of common sense which opposes it, at least serves to modify and restrain it”, and it goes straight to Ogilby against Milton and Bunyan against Addison. The essay exists to establish a standard of taste; the sentence is the position the essay is written to restrain. This is exactly the trap the brief lists twice, under Beauty will save the world (Ippolit reporting Myshkin) and To thine own self be true (Polonius), and the brief's closing instruction is general: a line one voice REPORTS of another is the reporter's, and the note says so. The note here is empty, so the card would print a doctrine Hume introduces as somebody else's as if it were his morning counsel. Not refuted as a forgery, refuted as shipped: it cannot go out with a blank note. Second, smaller defect: “para. 7 (Miller edition, pp. 229 to 230)” welds two systems, since the paragraph number is Digital Hume's editorial numbering and the Miller print edition numbers no paragraphs. Drop the paragraph number and keep the pages, which locate it on their own. Everything else checks: shipped.js clean, Hume 0 of 3, not banned, in scope, publishable, tag Essay correct, and the proposal rightly restores the colon and the trailing clause that Calendar For Life candidate 82 had cut. A corrected version below, with a note that must travel with it: Hume sets this out as the sceptical case and then argues against its consequence, so if the editor wants it as counsel the note has to say so, or drop it for a sentence Hume asserts in his own voice.
betterCitation: David Hume, Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, Of the Standard of Taste (ed. Miller, pp. 229 to 230)
